1: You check the stranger's timer: 12403. You tip extra. You scan the subway car. Mother: 42. Baby: 19801. So you give up your seat. You stare at your sister across the table. Her timer blinks 14. You haven't spoken in three years. What if you could see a death count above everyone's head? You'd finally know who matters. One catch: the timer counts whoever you're thinking of — right now. That's real. Part one.
2: Part one was the fun part. Now you test it. Rule one: the number follows your thoughts. You think of the barista. At home. In bed. His number appears. 12403. He's not even here. You don't need to see them. You need to think of them. You write a number down before you look. 9412. You look. 9412. It's real. You test it ten times. Ten times, you're right. Rule two: the numbers tick down. In real time. You watch a stranger's number. It drops. One second at a time. Rule three: you can't turn it off. You close your eyes. The numbers are still there. At school, the man in the charcoal suit finds you. His timer says 8912. He's been watching you watch him. "What are you staring at?" "Nothing." "You've been staring at me for a minute." You walk away. Fast. It's real. All of it.
3: So you start testing everyone. Your best friend, Sam. Orange hoodie. Always has your back. You check Sam. 15204. He saves you the last slice of pizza every Friday. "What?" "Nothing." Mr. Ortiz, the janitor. You check him. 9412. He waters the dead plant by the gym door every morning. "Morning." "It'll come back." Maya, the quiet girl in the library. You check her. 17842. She writes a novel in a notebook she never lets anyone read. "It's not finished." You see the mother again. On the same subway. Her number says 41. Yesterday it said 42. The baby still says 19801. The numbers are real. They move. You start doing small kindnesses. For the small numbers. You carry Mr. Ortiz's boxes. You hold doors. You give up seats. It feels good. Like you finally know what to do with it. You check the whole cafeteria. Hundreds of numbers. All at once. Most are big. Thousands of days. Years and years. A few are small. Too small. You look away. And then you see the pattern. The numbers are brightest over the people you already know. The strangers are dim. Like a light turned low. The people you love burn bright. You feel like you have a superpower. You can finally see who matters. You just don't know what "matters" costs yet.
4: This next bit is real. Now, the strange part. Start with 100,000 babies. That's how the CDC counts a lifetime. Most of them get about 28,500 days. The average American gets about 78 years. The CDC counted it in 2023. Some get less. A few get more. The baby has 19,801. Your sister has 14. In 1999, a scientist at Stanford named Laura Carstensen asked a simple question. What do people do when time runs out? She found that when people feel time is short, they stop chasing new things. They choose the people they love. In 2017, researchers gave sixty workers 40 dollars each. One weekend, buy a thing. The next weekend, buy time. Sixty workers, two weekends, forty dollars each. The time weekend won. Every time. People who buy back time are happier than people who buy things. The timers? Those are ours. Nobody has ever seen one. But the way they change you? That's real. That is what the timer does to you. It makes every day feel like the last one.
5: And then you start using it. You tell Sam his number. You think you're helping. "Fifteen thousand, two hundred and four days," you say. "That's forty-one years. Use them." He laughs. Then he stops. He stops applying to college. "Then why bother?" he says. You try to take it back. You can't. The number is in his head now. Sam stops texting back. You see him in the hallway. His number is the same. He is not. You avoid your sister. Fourteen is too bright to look at. You take the long way to class. You eat lunch in the library. Three years of silence becomes hiding. You start sorting people. You sit next to the big numbers. You walk past the small ones. You catch yourself doing it. And you feel sick. When you can see everyone's ending, you stop seeing the people. You just see the countdown. You know everyone's ending. And you've never felt more alone. At night, you see the numbers through the ceiling. Through the walls. Through the dark.
6: That night, you look in the mirror. Nothing above your head. You turn. You stand on a chair. You hold up your phone. Nothing. You ask Sam what he sees. "Nothing," he says. "Just you." You try everything. The bathroom mirror. The window. A shop window. A puddle. A photo. Nothing. You flip through old photos. Every head is blank. Even yours. Even then. Every photo. Every year. Every single one. You climb to the roof at dusk. The city glows with numbers. Yours is blank. The one number you actually want, the only one that matters, you'll never get. You can't see your own.
7: That's when you test it properly. You stare at the man in the charcoal suit. You think of nothing but him. His number stays dim. Flickering. Hard to read. 8912. Like a light turned low. You try to picture the barista's face. You can't. His number is a faint smudge. 12403. Barely there. You think of your sister. You don't even have to look. Fourteen burns so bright it hurts. You'd finally know who matters. You were right. You just had it backwards. The timer never showed you everyone's death. It only ever showed you the person at the front of your mind. It was never about their endings. It was about your attention. The numbers are a map of who you love. Every number you've seen was someone you were already carrying with you. Your whole week was a map. The barista. The mother. The baby. Sam. Maya. Mr. Ortiz. The brightest numbers are the people you love most. Because those are the endings you already feel. You were never counting their days. You were counting your love.
8: "Go talk to her," Sam says. So you go to the diner. The same booth. Dusk through the window. Two coffees. Still untouched. Your sister is there. Her timer says 14. You sit down. You speak. First words in three years. "You came." "I missed you." The number doesn't change. Fourteen is still fourteen. But you stop counting. You ask her about her day. She laughs. You forgot what that sounds like. You stay for an hour. Then two. She tells you about school. About her friends. About the book she's reading. You tell her about the numbers. She doesn't laugh. She just listens. For the first time in three years, the table doesn't feel like a wall. You can't add days to her number. But you can fill the days in it. The timer is still there. But you're not looking at it anymore. You're looking at her. Connections give our days meaning. The days don't matter. The people do. The next morning, you sit with Sam at lunch. And Maya. You don't check anyone's number. Outside, the city glows with numbers. Thousands of them. All at once. You don't count them anymore. You just walk home. With your sister. She talks the whole way. You let her. Fourteen days. You plan to use every one of them. So... what would yours say? Tell us in the comments.
